items.q: Which acquisitions are exempt from the part 6 competition requirements?
items.a: Contracts awarded using the simplified acquisition procedures of part 13; procedures expressly authorized by statute; in-scope modifications (including exercising priced options evaluated in the original competition); and orders under requirements, definite-quantity, indefinite-quantity, and task- or delivery-order contracts.

cite.quote: This part applies to all acquisitions except— (a) Contracts awarded using the simplified acquisition procedures of part 13; (b) Contracts awarded using contracting procedures (other than those addressed in this part) that are expressly authorized by statute

items.q: Name the seven statutory exceptions permitting other than full and open competition.
items.a: Only one responsible source; unusual and compelling urgency; industrial mobilization, engineering/developmental/research capability, or expert services; international agreement; authorized or required by statute; national security; and public interest (RFO 6.103-1 through 6.103-7).

cite.quote: Agencies may contract without providing for full and open competition under authorities specified in this section (see 10 U.S.C. 3204 and 41 U.S.C. 3304).

items.q: May other than full and open competition be justified by a lack of planning or a shortage of funds?
items.a: No. It must not be justified on the basis of a lack of planning by the requiring activity or concerns about the amount of funds available to the agency or activity.

cite.quote: Contracting without providing for full and open competition must not be justified on the basis of— (1) A lack of planning by the requiring activity; or (2) Concerns related to the amount of funds available to the agency or activity for acquisition.

items.q: Which two competition exceptions do not require a justification and approval?
items.a: Authorized or required by statute (6.103-5) and public interest (6.103-7). Every other 6.103 authority requires the justification and approval at 6.104.

cite.quote: A justification and approval must support procedures under 6.103, except 6.103-5 and 6.103-7.

items.q: Under the one-responsible-source exception, when may a follow-on for a major system be sole-sourced?
items.a: When award to another source would result in substantial duplication of cost to the Government not expected to be recovered through competition, or unacceptable delays in fulfilling the agency's requirements.

cite.quote: (i) Substantial duplication of cost to the Government that is not expected to be recovered through competition; or (ii) Unacceptable delays in fulfilling the agency's requirements.

items.q: Does a brand-name purchase description restrict competition? What about brand-name or equal?
items.a: A pure brand-name description (or attributes peculiar to one manufacturer) prevents full and open competition and must be justified and approved under 6.104. Brand-name-or-equal descriptions provide for full and open competition.

cite.quote: use of brand-name descriptions, or specification of attributes peculiar to one manufacturer, prevents full and open competition and should only be used when justified and approved according to 6.104. This does not apply to “brand name or equal” descriptions as they provide for full and open competition.

items.q: How long may a contract awarded under the urgency exception run?
items.a: No longer than needed to meet the urgent requirement and to competitively award a follow-on — and not more than one year including all options, unless the head of the agency determines exceptional circumstances apply.

cite.quote: May not exceed one year, including all options, unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply.

items.q: Recite the justification approval ladder.
items.a: Up to $900,000 — the contracting officer (the 6.104(a)(12) certification is the approval). Over $900,000 to $20 million — advocate for competition, not delegable. Over $20 million to $90 million ($150 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard) — head of the procuring activity. Above that — senior procurement executive. Include the value of all options when setting the level.

cite.quote: $900,000 or below Contracting officer. Accomplished by certification required at 6.104(a)(12). >$900,000 - $20,000,000 Advocate for competition. Not delegable.

items.q: When must a justification for other than full and open competition be posted publicly?
items.a: Within 14 days after contract award — except urgency (6.103-2) justifications post within 30 days, and brand-name justifications post with the solicitation.

cite.quote: The justification must be made publicly available within 14 days after contract award, except— (1) Justifications under 6.103-2 must be posted within 30 days after contract award

items.q: Does full and open competition after excluding sources (for example, a set-aside) require its own justification and approval?
items.a: No. It still uses the competitive procedures of 6.101 among the narrowed field, and requires no separate justification and approval or determination and findings.

cite.quote: Acquisitions under this section do not require separate justification and approval or determination and findings.

items.q: When may sealed bidding be used instead of competitive proposals?
items.a: Only when all four conditions hold: time permits soliciting, submitting, and evaluating sealed bids; award will be made on price and price-related factors; discussions with bidders are unnecessary; and more than one sealed bid is reasonably expected.

cite.quote: (i) Time permits staff to solicit, submit, and evaluate sealed bids; (ii) The award will be made on the basis of price and other price-related factors; (iii) Discussion with bidders is unnecessary; and (iv) Contracting officers reasonably expect to receive more than one sealed bid.

items.q: What is the baseline ordering rule on a multiple-award contract?
items.a: Each awardee must be given a fair opportunity to be considered for every order or BPA valued above the micro-purchase threshold, unless a sole-source order is justified and approved under 16.507-6.

cite.quote: The contracting officer must provide each awardee a fair opportunity to be considered for each order or BPA valued above the micro-purchase threshold according to paragraph (c) and 16.507-3 through 16.507-5, unless a sole source order or BPA is justified and approved according to 16.507-6.

items.q: Are task orders subject to part 6 competition or the subpart 15.3 source selection rules?
items.a: No. The ordering process is not subject to part 6, subpart 15.3, or part 14 — streamlined procedures are allowed, with no required evaluation plans, scoring, or competitive range.

cite.quote: The ordering process is not subject to the competition requirements in part 6 or the policies in subpart 15.3 or part 14.

items.q: Name the exceptions that allow a sole-source order despite fair opportunity.
items.a: Urgency causing unacceptable delays; only one awardee capable (unique or highly specialized); logical follow-on in the interest of economy and efficiency; satisfying a minimum guarantee; a statute authorizing a specified source (orders over the SAT); and, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, the 6.103 exceptions.

cite.quote: (1) The agency need for the supplies or services is so urgent that providing a fair opportunity would result in unacceptable delays. (2) Only one awardee is capable of providing the supplies or services required at the level of quality required because the supplies or services ordered are unique or highly specialized. (3) The order must be issued on a sole-source basis in the interest of economy and efficiency because it is a logical follow-on to an order already issued under the contract, provided that all awardees were given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order. (4) It is necessary to place an order to satisfy a minimum guarantee.

items.q: What condition is built into the logical-follow-on exception?
items.a: All awardees must have been given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order — and the justification must describe why the relationship between the initial order and the follow-on is logical.

cite.quote: it is a logical follow-on to an order already issued under the contract, provided that all awardees were given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order.

items.q: Who hears a contract holder's complaint about order placement?
items.a: The agency's task-order and delivery-order ombudsman — a senior official independent of the contracting officer who reviews complaints and ensures awardees are afforded a fair opportunity consistent with the contract's procedures.

cite.quote: The head of the agency must designate a task-order and delivery-order ombudsman. The ombudsman must review complaints from contractors and ensure they are afforded a fair opportunity to be considered, consistent with the procedures in the contract.

items.q: What must the fair notice include for orders above $7.5 million?
items.a: A clear statement of the agency's requirements, a reasonable response period, and disclosure of the significant evaluation factors and subfactors — including cost or price — and their relative importance.

cite.quote: Orders valued above $7.5 million (a) Procedures . Provide a fair notice of the intent to place an order to all contractors offering the products or services according to 16.507-4. A fair notice must— (1) Include a clear statement of the agency’s requirements; (2) Allow for a reasonable response period; and (3) Disclose the significant factors and subfactors, as applicable, including cost or price, that the agency expects to consider in evaluating quotations, offers, or other responses to notices, and their relative importance;

items.q: Do losing contract holders get a debriefing on large task orders?
items.a: Yes — for orders in the above-$7.5 million tier, postaward notifications and debriefings follow part 15, and a summary of the debriefing goes in the order file.

cite.quote: (c) Postaward notices and debriefings. Provide postaward notifications and debriefings according to part 15. A summary of the debriefing must be included in the task or delivery order file.

items.q: When can a task or delivery order be protested?
items.a: Only on grounds that the order increases the scope, period, or maximum value of the contract — or, at GAO only, for orders valued over $35 million (DoD, NASA, Coast Guard) or $10 million (other agencies).

cite.quote: (1) A protest on the grounds that the order increases the scope, period, or maximum value of the contract; or (2) (i) For agencies other than DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, a protest of an order valued in excess of $10 million (41 U.S.C. 4106(f)); or (ii) For DoD, NASA, or the Coast Guard, a protest of an order valued in excess of $35 million (10 U.S.C. 3406(f)).

items.q: What makes an indefinite-quantity contract binding?
items.a: The stated minimum quantity the Government must order — it must be more than a nominal quantity, but should not exceed the amount the Government is fairly certain to order.

cite.quote: The contract must require the Government to order and the contractor to furnish at least a stated minimum quantity of supplies or services. To ensure that the contract is binding, the minimum quantity must be more than a nominal quantity, but it should not exceed the amount that the Government is fairly certain to order.

items.q: Single award or multiple awards on an indefinite-quantity solicitation?
items.a: Multiple awards are preferred to the maximum extent practicable, with the decision documented — and a single-award task- or delivery-order contract estimated over $150 million (including options) requires a written head-of-agency determination.

cite.quote: No task or delivery order contract in an amount estimated to exceed $150 million (including all options) may be awarded to a single source unless the head of the agency determines in writing

items.q: Can an order under a multiple-award contract be set aside for small business?
items.a: Yes — contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders for small business concerns, and that discretionary decision is not itself a basis for protest.

cite.quote: contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders placed under multiple-award contracts for any of the small business concerns identified in 19.000(a)(3).

items.q: How long may a DoD task- or delivery-order contract run?
items.a: Up to five years, extendable by option or modification — but the total period as extended may not exceed 10 years unless the head of the agency determines in writing that exceptional circumstances require a longer period.

cite.quote: may provide for the contract to cover any period up to five years and may extend the contract period for one or more successive periods pursuant to an option provided in the contract or a modification of the contract. The total contract period as extended may not exceed 10 years unless such head of an agency determines in writing that exceptional circumstances necessitate a longer contract period.

items.q: List the determinations required before exercising an option.
items.a: Written notice within the contract's specified time; funds available; the option fulfills an existing Government requirement; it was synopsized unless exempt; no active SAM exclusion; acceptable performance on the current contract; the price is fair and reasonable under current market conditions and exercise is in the Government's best interest; and the exercise complies with part 6.

cite.quote: (1) Providing written notice to the contractor of the Government’s intention to exercise the option, within the time specified in the contract; (2) Confirming that funds are available; and (3) Determining that– (i) The option fulfills an existing Government requirement; (ii) The option was synopsized as required, unless exempt (see part 5); (iii) The Contractor does not have an active exclusion record in the System for Award Management (see part 9); (iv) The contractor’s performance on the current contract has been acceptable

items.q: Why does exercising an option not require a new competition?
items.a: Because the exercise must comply with part 6 by having been evaluated as part of the initial competition and being exercisable at an amount specified in, or reasonably determinable from, the terms of the contract.

cite.quote: The option exercise complies with the requirements of part 6 for full and open competition, i.e., the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the terms of the contract.

items.q: When are options prohibited?
items.a: When the price or availability of necessary material or labor is not reasonably foreseeable — introducing significant option-pricing risk — or when market prices for the supplies or services are likely to change significantly.

cite.quote: The contracting officer must not use options when- (1) Price or availability of necessary material or labor is not reasonably foreseeable, introducing significant risk into option pricing; or (2) Market prices for the supplies or services are likely to change significantly.

items.q: How far can the Option to Extend Services clause stretch a service contract?
items.a: It may be exercised more than once, but the total extension of performance may not exceed 6 months, at the rates specified in the contract.

cite.quote: The option provision may be exercised more than once, but the total extension of performance hereunder shall not exceed 6 months.

items.q: After market research, in what order of priority must an agency source its requirement?
items.a: (1) A commercial product or service on an existing governmentwide contract; (2) modify the requirement so an existing governmentwide contract can be used; (3) a commercial product or service from another source; (4) a commercial product or service that could be modified; and only then (5) a nondevelopmental item.

cite.quote: (1) A commercial product or commercial service on an existing governmentwide contract can meet the agency's requirements; (2) The requirements could be modified so the agency could use an existing governmentwide contract; (3) A commercial product or commercial service is available from another source; (4) A commercial product or commercial service could be modified to meet the agency's requirements; or (5) The requirement can only be satisfied by a nondevelopmental item.

items.q: How much information may you ask potential sources for during market research, and how is the research documented?
items.a: No more than the minimum information necessary to make the required determinations — and the results must be documented in a manner that suits the acquisition's size and complexity.

cite.quote: When conducting market research, agencies must not ask potential sources to submit more than the minimum information necessary to make the determinations required in paragraph (f).

items.q: What does restricting competition on a commercial acquisition over the SAT require?
items.a: A written justification approved as described in 6.104, citing the applicable statutory authority. At or below the SAT, documenting the single-source decision and its basis suffices.

cite.quote: For acquisitions valued over the SAT, prepare a written justification and obtain approval of the justification as described in 6.104.

items.q: How are commercial acquisitions over $9 million solicited?
items.a: Using the subpart 12.2 procedures in conjunction with part 15 (requests for proposals) or part 14 (invitations for bids) — with the RFP preferred because it considers past performance.

cite.quote: For acquisitions valued at greater than $9 million, use the procedures in this subpart in conjunction with the procedures in part 15 for requests for proposals (RFPs) or part 14 for invitations for bids (IFBs), as appropriate.

items.q: How detailed do commercial evaluation factors need to be?
items.a: For most commercial acquisitions, no more detailed than technical (capability of the products or services to meet the need), price, and past performance — predetermined technical subfactors are not required.

cite.quote: For most acquisitions of commercial products or commercial services, evaluation factors need not be more detailed than technical (capability of the products or services offered to meet the agency’s needs), price, and past performance.

items.q: Which termination machinery applies to commercial contracts?
items.a: The termination paragraphs of clause 52.212-4 — not part 49. And before terminating for cause, send a cure notice unless the reason is late delivery.

cite.quote: Follow the procedures in this section and the termination paragraphs of the clause at 52.212-4, when terminating contracts for commercial products or commercial services. Do not use the procedures in part 49.

items.q: Which contract types are the default?
items.a: Fixed-price types are the default and preferred. If a fixed-price type is not appropriate for the entire contract, consider whether a portion of it can be established on a fixed-price basis.

cite.quote: Fixed-price contract types are the default and preferred contract types. If a fixed-price contract type is not appropriate for an entire contract, consider whether a portion of the contract can be established on a fixed-price basis.

items.q: When must firm-fixed-price be used, and what if a reasonable basis for firm pricing does not exist?
items.a: FFP must be used when the risk involved is minimal or predictable with an acceptable degree of certainty. Without a firm pricing basis, select a type (or combination) that appropriately ties profit to contractor performance.

cite.quote: A firm-fixed-price contract (see section 16.202) must be used when the risk involved is minimal or can be predicted with an acceptable degree of certainty.

items.q: What gates must a cost-reimbursement contract clear before award?
items.a: A written acquisition plan approved at least one level above the contracting officer; the agency-head justification for other than fixed-price if 16.104 requires it; a contractor accounting system that can segregate, accumulate, and allocate contract costs; and sufficient Government resources — including a designated COR — to manage it.

cite.quote: (1) A written acquisition plan has been approved at least one level above the contracting officer (see 7.102(d)); (2) The agency head approves a justification for other than fixed-price contracts, if required by 16.104. (3) The contractor’s accounting system can adequately segregate, accumulate and allocate costs specifically attributed to the contract or order during contract performance

items.q: At what values does the Executive Order 14402 other-than-fixed-price justification apply?
items.a: $100 million for DoD, $35 million for NASA, $25 million for DHS, and $10 million for all other Federal agencies — approved by the head of the agency before using a covered contract or order.

cite.quote: a justification is required for covered contracts and orders valued at or above— (i) $100 million, for DoD; (ii) $35 million, for NASA; (iii) $25 million, for Department of Homeland Security; or (iv) $10 million, for all other Federal agencies.

items.q: What distinguishes a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract?
items.a: The fixed fee does not change with actual cost — it may be adjusted only as a result of changes in the work to be performed under the contract.

cite.quote: A cost-plus-fixed-fee contract is a cost-reimbursement contract that includes payment of an agreed upon fixed-fee. The fixed fee does not change with actual cost but may be adjusted as a result of changes in the work to be performed under the contract.

items.q: What elements does a fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract specify, and who absorbs cost above the price ceiling?
items.a: A target cost, a target profit, a price ceiling (but no profit ceiling or floor), and a profit-adjustment formula. If final negotiated cost exceeds the price ceiling, the contractor absorbs the difference as a loss.

cite.quote: A fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract specifies a target cost, a target profit, a price ceiling (but not a profit ceiling or floor), and a formula for profit adjustments. When the final cost is less than the target cost, application of the formula results in a final profit greater than the target profit; conversely, when final cost is more than target cost, application of the formula results in a final profit less than the target profit, or even a net loss. If the final negotiated cost exceeds the price ceiling, the contractor absorbs the difference as a loss.

items.q: What are the HUBZone sole-source dollar caps?
items.a: $8.5 million for requirements in manufacturing NAICS codes and $5.5 million for all other NAICS codes — with no reasonable expectation of offers from two or more HUBZone concerns, a responsible contractor, and award at a fair and reasonable price.

cite.quote: The anticipated price of the contract, including options, will not exceed— (i) $8.5 million for a requirement within the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes for manufacturing; or (ii) $5.5 million for a requirement within all other NAICS codes

items.q: When must an 8(a) acquisition be competed among 8(a) participants?
items.a: When there is a reasonable expectation that at least two eligible, responsible 8(a) participants will offer at a fair market price, and the anticipated total value including options exceeds $8.5 million for manufacturing NAICS codes or $5.5 million for all other acquisitions.

cite.quote: The anticipated total value of the contract, including options, will exceed $8.5 million for acquisitions assigned manufacturing North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes and $5.5 million for all other acquisitions.

items.q: What extra scrutiny applies to a sole-source 8(a) award above the competitive threshold — and above $30 million?
items.a: Above the competitive threshold, SBA may accept the requirement sole-source only after the contracting officer complies with 6.103. For sole-source 8(a) contracts over $30 million, the justification must include at minimum the description and estimated value, the statutory authority, and the fair-and-reasonable-cost determination.

cite.quote: For sole-source 8(a) contracts over $30 million, the justification must include, at a minimum, the contents described at paragraphs (a)(3), (a)(4), and (a)(7) of this section.

items.q: Once SBA accepts a requirement into the 8(a) program, can the follow-on be competed outside it?
items.a: Not unilaterally. Follow-on requirements stay in the 8(a) program unless there is a mandatory source, the follow-on is set aside under the HUBZone, SDVOSB, or WOSB programs, or SBA agrees in writing to release the requirement.

cite.quote: Once a requirement has been accepted by SBA into the 8(a) program, any follow-on requirements (see definition at 13 CFR 124.3) must remain in the 8(a) program unless

items.q: You find the apparent successful small business nonresponsible. Can you just award to the next offeror?
items.a: No — withhold award and refer the small business to SBA for a possible Certificate of Competency, even if the next acceptable offer is also from a small business.

cite.quote: If a contracting officer determines an apparent successful small business offeror to be nonresponsible, the contracting officer must refer that small business to SBA for a possible COC, even if the next acceptable offer is from a small business.

items.q: How final is an SBA Certificate of Competency?
items.a: Final as to all elements of responsibility — a certified concern must not be held to any other responsibility requirements, though award may still be withheld for reasons unrelated to responsibility. If SBA has not issued the COC within 15 business days of the referral, award goes to another appropriately selected, responsible offeror.

cite.quote: SBA COCs are final with respect to all elements of responsibility of prospective small business contractors. An SBA-certified concern must not be required to meet any other requirements of responsibility.

items.q: When does a subcontracting plan become a condition of award?
items.a: In acquisitions expected to exceed $900,000 ($2 million for construction of a public facility) with subcontracting possibilities, the apparently successful other-than-small offeror must submit an acceptable subcontracting plan or be ineligible for award.

cite.quote: each solicitation of offers to perform a contract that is expected to exceed $900,000 ($2 million for construction of any public facility) and that has subcontracting possibilities, must require the apparently successful offeror to submit an acceptable subcontracting plan.
